section.title: Python Exceptions in Rexx
section.para: A Python exception raised by a call from Rexx is the condition SYNTAX 98.900, whose message is Python error: followed by the exception's type and text: Python error: TypeError: .... Its condition object has, in the ADDITIONAL Array:

listitem.para: the traceback, as Python formats it (an empty string for an exception raised with , which has none yet).

section.para: This is the layout of BSF4ooRexx, whose additional[2] is the Java exception.
Rexx code traps it as any SYNTAX condition, with signal on syntax or call on syntax.

example.title: A Python exception, trapped in Rexx
example.programlisting:
signal on syntax say .py~int("seven") exit syntax: c = condition("O") say c~code say c~message e = c~additional[2] -- the exception say .py~type(e)~getattr("__name__") e~args
::requires "python.cls"
example.screen: 98.900 Python error: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'seven'. ValueError ("invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'seven'",)

section.title: Raising Python Exceptions from Rexx
section.para: raises a Python exception from Rexx code: an exception object, or an exception class called with the remaining arguments. In Rexx it is the same SYNTAX 98.900 as when Python raises it.

example.title: .py~raise
example.programlisting:
signal on syntax .py~raise(.py~KeyError, "missing") syntax: say condition("O")~message say .py~isinstance(condition("O")~additional[2], .py~KeyError)
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Exceptions that Go Back to Python
section.para: A Python exception that goes through Rexx code back to Python is raised again as itself. Python calls Rexx (a callback, an override of a class that extends a Python class, a routine), the Rexx code calls Python, which raises; if the Rexx code does not trap the condition, the Python caller gets the original exception, with its traceback. Python's protocols depend on it: a sequence ends with IndexError, an iterator with StopIteration, a mapping says "missing" with KeyError.

The other way round, a Rexx condition that goes through Python back to Rexx is raised again as itself. Rexx calls Python (a function, an ADDRESS environment written in Python), Python calls Rexx code that fails, and if Python does not catch the , the Rexx caller gets the original condition, not SYNTAX 98.900: a SYNTAX error with its code and message, any other condition with its description, ADDITIONAL and result. With ooRexx 5.3.0 r13278, only SYNTAX errors leave Rexx code that Python calls, and ooRexx does not give a native caller a USER, NOTREADY, ERROR or FAILURE condition that the Rexx code does not trap.

A HALT is SYNTAX 4.1 by the time it leaves that Rexx code (Python sees Rexx error 4.1), and back in Rexx it is a HALT again, as a Ctrl-C would be: SIGNAL ON HALT traps it at the end of the clause that called Python, CALL ON HALT runs its handler after the next clause (the call gives .nil meanwhile), and a caller that does not trap HALT gets SYNTAX 4.1, as in plain Rexx. Its description, ADDITIONAL and result are lost on the way: ooRexx drops them when it turns the HALT into 4.1.

section.title: Rexx Conditions in Python
section.para: Any other Rexx condition that reaches Python, an error in Rexx code that Python called, is an , whose text is Rexx's message: Rexx error 42.3: Arithmetic overflow; divisor must not be zero. Its attributes are the parts of the condition: its code, its line, its program, its texts and its traceback ().

example.title: Rexx errors and Python exceptions, seen from Python
example.screen: RexxError True Rexx error 42.3: Arithmetic overflow; divisor must not be zero. KeyError 'nope'
